abstract: Luis Garicano argues that conflating task automation with job extinction is a fundamental analytical error. A job is a bundle of tasks, and whether AI eliminates a job depends not on whether it can perform one component but on whether that component can be separated from the rest at low cost. Garicano identifies three conditions that keep job bundles intact: unpredictable demand (customer service calls that seem routine often reveal deeper issues, making constant AI-to-human handoffs expensive), production spillovers (radiologists reading scans after patient consultation outperform those viewing images alone), and measurement problems (accountability becomes unclear when AI drafts and humans sign). He cites two powerful empirical cases: travel agents, where despite online booking eliminating 60% of employment, surviving agents moved upmarket with weekly earnings rising from 87% to 99% of the private-sector average between 2000 and 2025; and accountants, where Frey and Osborne's 2013 prediction of 94% automation probability was contradicted by BLS data showing 1.6 million employed accountants with 5% projected growth through 2034. The author invokes Kenneth Arrow on trust and Oliver Williamson on relationship-specific investments to explain why managers exercise 'residual decision rights' that require accountability, legitimacy rituals, and reputational stakes AI cannot currently provide.
keyFindings: Jobs are bundles of tasks; automating one task does not eliminate the job if the task cannot be separated from the bundle at low cost.
Three conditions strengthen job bundles against AI unbundling: unpredictable demand, production spillovers, and measurement/accountability problems.
Travel agents lost 60% of employment to online booking but survivors moved upmarket, with earnings rising from 87% to 99% of the private-sector average (2000-2025).
Despite a 2013 prediction of 94% automation probability, BLS counts 1.6 million accountants with 5% projected growth through 2034.
Managers exercise 'residual decision rights' — authority over unforeseen situations — that require accountability and legitimacy AI cannot yet provide.
methodology: Economic analysis drawing on task-based labor economics, organizational theory (Arrow, Williamson), and empirical case studies of occupations predicted for automation. Uses BLS occupational employment data and historical wage comparisons.
qualifiers: The analysis focuses on why current AI may not eliminate entire occupations, but does not address whether future AI systems could overcome the bundling barriers identified. Travel agents and accountants are specific cases that may not generalize to all occupations. The piece is a conceptual essay rather than a quantitative empirical study. Does not account for the possibility that employers may restructure job bundles specifically to enable AI substitution.
